### 01 · Just been told
Group: **The first days** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

*Carries an emergency or same-day line: rendered open, never collapsed, and every figure on it renders in both locales.*

- There’s no right way to feel about this news, and no need to take it all in at once `1.1`
- Diabetes Canada says depression is more common in people with diabetes, so looking after your mood is part of looking after your diabetes `1.2`
- Diabetes Canada’s guideline says diabetes teams should ask everyone, from time to time, about diabetes distress and about mood and anxiety. You can bring it up first `1.3`
- Your team will start with what you need to know first. The rest can wait `1.4`

> **Note** `1.note` — If it isn’t easing, tell your diabetes team or your doctor. If you’d like to talk to a mental health professional, Breakthrough T1D keeps a Mental Health + Diabetes Directory of registered providers.

*Sources for this card:* Taking care of your mental health (Diabetes Canada); Mental Health and Diabetes: 2023 Update (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Mental Health Support (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); 9-8-8: Suicide Crisis Helpline (9-8-8: Suicide Crisis Helpline (Canada))

### 02 · Which diabetes is this?
Group: **The first days** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

- Type 1: the pancreas doesn’t make insulin. Diabetes Canada says 5 to 10% of people with diabetes have type 1, and it can start in adulthood too `2.1`
- Type 2: the most common type, 90 to 95% of people with diabetes. It may have no symptoms `2.2`
- Gestational diabetes: shows up during pregnancy, in 3 to 20% of pregnancies. It usually goes away after the birth, but it raises the chance of type 2 later, for you and your child `2.3`
- Prediabetes: blood sugar that’s higher than normal, but not yet high enough to be called type 2 diabetes `2.4`
- Less common types: Diabetes Canada’s guideline lists less common forms, such as LADA (which it counts as type 1) and monogenic diabetes, and says some cases are hard to classify. If your type doesn’t seem to fit, ask your team `2.5`

> **Note** `2.note` — Know Your Type has a card for each one, including the less common types.

*Sources for this card:* Type 1 Diabetes (Diabetes Canada); Type 2 Diabetes (Diabetes Canada); Gestational Diabetes (Diabetes Canada); Prediabetes (Diabetes Canada); Definition, Classification and Diagnosis of Diabetes, Prediabetes and Metabolic Syndrome (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines)

### 03 · Your target ranges
Group: **The first days** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

- Diabetes Canada’s usual targets are 4.0 to 7.0 mmol/L before meals and 5.0 to 10.0 two hours after eating `3.1`
- If your A1C isn’t at target, your team may set a lower after-meal target, weighing it against the risk of lows. Diabetes Canada gives 5.0 to 8.0 ✎ `3.2`
- A1C is a blood test that shows your average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months. It’s usually done about every 3 months, and Diabetes Canada’s usual target is 7.0% or less `3.3`
- If you use a sensor, Diabetes Canada’s guideline uses international targets: for most adults, more than 70% of the day between 3.9 and 10.0 `3.4`
- Your team may set different targets, for example for children, or if you’re pregnant, frail, or often have severe lows `3.5`

> **Note** `3.note` — Write your own targets on the card and keep it with your meter. If your team gave you different numbers, use theirs.

*Sources for this card:* Checking Blood Sugar (Diabetes Canada); Targets for Glycemic Control (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Blood Glucose Monitoring in Adults and Children with Diabetes: Update 2021 (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Diabetes and Pregnancy (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Time in Range (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF))

### 04 · Food and movement: first steps
Group: **The first days** · Referral chip: **Ask a dietitian** · Products shown: *none*

- Canada’s food guide suggests plenty of vegetables and fruit, whole grains and protein foods, with plant protein more often `4.1`
- It suggests water as your drink of choice, and limiting highly processed foods `4.2`
- Diabetes Canada’s guideline supports more than one way of eating, including Mediterranean, DASH and vegetarian. A dietitian can help you find what fits `4.3`
- Start slowly, with 5 to 10 minutes of activity a day, and build up `4.4`
- Diabetes Canada suggests working up to 150 minutes a week of moderate to vigorous activity, such as 30 minutes on 5 days `4.5`
- If you haven’t been active for a while, talk to your doctor before you start anything harder than a brisk walk `4.6`
- If you take insulin or other medicines that lower blood sugar, carry fast-acting sugar when you’re active `4.7`

> **Note** `4.note` — Carb counting, eating out and more on moving your body are in Everyday Liivving. If you take insulin, ask your team how to plan around activity. ✎

*Sources for this card:* Healthy eating recommendations (Health Canada); Nutrition Therapy (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Exercise & Activity (Diabetes Canada); Physical Activity and Diabetes (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines)

### 05 · Supporting someone newly diagnosed
Group: **The first days** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

- Ask what help they’d like. Some people want company at appointments, and some would rather manage on their own `5.1`
- Learn what a low looks like for them, and where they keep fast-acting sugar. The steps are in The Rule of 15, in Staying Safe `5.2`
- If they’re at risk of a severe low, such as people who take insulin, Diabetes Canada’s guideline says the people around them should be taught to call 911, and how to give glucagon. The signs that need emergency care are in Staying Safe ✎ `5.3`
- If they have type 1, immediate family aged 2 to 45, and other relatives aged 2 to 20, can ask about free research screening through TrialNet, anywhere in Canada. The details are in Type 1 starts before symptoms, in Know Your Type ✎ `5.4`
- Your own feelings count too. If you’re caring for a child or teen with type 1, Breakthrough T1D has a Caregiver Guide `5.5`

> **Note** `5.note` — More for families and caregivers is in This Might Be You.

*Sources for this card:* Chapter 14: 2023 Update – Hypoglycemia in Adults (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Getting Started with Insulin (Diabetes Canada); TrialNet (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); Mental Health Support (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF))

### 06 · Do I need a meter?
Group: **Setting up** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes educator** · Products shown: *none*

- Whether you check your blood sugar at home, and how often, depends on your type and your treatment. Your team will tell you what you need `6.1`
- If you take insulin more than once a day, Diabetes Canada’s guideline says to check at least 3 times a day `6.2`
- For type 1 on injections or a pump, Diabetes Canada’s guidelines recommend a sensor that reads all the time (a continuous glucose monitor). Ask your team whether that fits you `6.3`
- A sensor can run up to 15 minutes behind your blood sugar, so Diabetes Canada suggests keeping a meter and strips as a backup `6.4`
- Choosing a meter, and the strips and lancets that go with it, is in Your Tools `6.5`

> **Note** `6.note` — Some provinces cover strips and sensors, and how much often depends on your treatment. Funding & Coverage has the details for your province.

*Sources for this card:* Blood Glucose Monitoring in Adults and Children with Diabetes: Update 2021 (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Checking Blood Sugar (Diabetes Canada); Technology & Devices (Diabetes Canada); Glycemic Management Across the Lifespan for People With Type 1 Diabetes (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Get coverage for prescription drugs (Government of Ontario); Comparisons by Province/Territory (Diabetes Canada)

### 07 · Your medicines and your pharmacist
Group: **Setting up** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist** · Products shown: *none*

- What is each of my medicines for, and when do I take it? `7.1`
- Can any of them cause a low? If so, what should I keep with me? `7.2`
- Do any of them need to be paused on a sick day? Diabetes Canada’s sick-day sheet has a space for your pharmacist to write this down `7.3`
- How do I store each one, and how long does it keep once it’s open? `7.4`
- Which supplies go with my medicines, and are they covered by my plan? `7.5`

> **Note** `7.note` — Take this list to your pharmacist or your next appointment, with your medicines or a list of them. Your prescriber chooses your medicines. Your pharmacist helps you use them safely.

*Sources for this card:* Stay Safe When You Have Diabetes and Are Sick or at Risk of Dehydration (Diabetes Canada); Getting Started with Insulin (Diabetes Canada)

### 08 · Starting insulin
Group: **Setting up** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes educator** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `startingInjections` — Nano PRO Pen Needles 4mm 32G (4777), EZH Oracle 32g 4mm Pen Needle (7544), Sharps Container 1L (4350)

- Diabetes Canada says everyone with type 1, and many people with type 2, need insulin to stay healthy `8.1`
- There’s no one-size-fits-all plan. Your team works out with you how many injections, when, how much, and whether a pump suits you `8.2`
- Insulin can be taken with a pen, a syringe or a pump. Pens come with an instruction book, so read it to learn how yours works `8.3`
- Change where you inject each time. Diabetes Canada says this helps prevent fatty lumps that can make insulin work poorly `8.4`
- Use a new pen tip or needle every time, then put it in a sharps container `8.5`
- Insulin raises your risk of a low. Diabetes Canada says to always have fast-acting sugar with you, at home and when you go out. The steps are in The Rule of 15, in Staying Safe `8.6`
- Storage is different for each insulin. Follow the leaflet that came with yours, or ask your pharmacist `8.7`
- Diabetes Canada says to throw out insulin that has been frozen, has been in temperatures over 30°C, or has expired `8.8`

> **Note** `8.note` — Your prescriber chooses your insulin, and fine-tuning your routine takes time. A step-by-step injection guide is in Your Tools.

*Sources for this card:* Getting Started with Insulin (Diabetes Canada)

*Links in the card’s own sentences. Navigation only: the link tags go around words already there and add none, so no French review gate holds them back.*

### 09 · Sharps from day one
Group: **Setting up** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist** · Products shown: *none*

- Used lancets, pen tips and needles go in a sharps container. Diabetes Canada says pen tips and needles are for one use only `9.1`
- Sharps include lancets, pen needles, sensor applicators that have a needle, infusion sets and syringes `9.2`
- Never put used sharps in the garbage or recycling, says the Health Products Stewardship Association `9.3`
- In Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, participating pharmacies give out free sharps containers and take them back `9.4`
- Elsewhere in Canada, ask your pharmacy. Diabetes Canada says many pharmacies supply containers and swap a full one for a new one `9.5`

> **Note** `9.note` — Ask your pharmacy where to return a full container near you.

*Sources for this card:* Returning Medical Sharps (Health Products Stewardship Association); Getting Started with Insulin (Diabetes Canada)

### 10 · Your starter supply list
Group: **Setting up** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist CDE** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `starterList` — `meters`: OneTouch Verio Reflect Meter (4287), Contour NEXT ONE Meter (4524), Accu-Chek Guide Meter (4556), FreeStyle Lite Meter (4402); `injections`: Nano PRO Pen Needles 4mm 32G (4777), EZH Oracle 32g 4mm Pen Needle (7544), Ultra-Fine Insulin Syringes 0.3mL (4655); `sensors`: Dexcom G7 Sensor 1-Pack (4227), FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus Sensor (4316); `everyone`: Dex4 Fast Acting Glucose Tablets Tropical Fruit (7371), Dex4 Glucose Gel Fruit Punch (7382), PharmaSystems Med ID Bracelet Diabetic (7778), Sharps Container 1L (4350)

- If you check with a meter: the meter, its strips and lancets, and a sharps container `10.1`
- If you take insulin: a new pen tip or needle for each injection, and a sharps container `10.2`
- If you take insulin: fast-acting sugar with you, at home and when you go out `10.3`
- A card in your wallet that says you have diabetes, or medical ID such as a bracelet or necklace `10.4`
- If you use a sensor: a meter and strips as a backup `10.5`
- If you use a pump: backup insulin pens or syringes, extra pump supplies, ketone strips or a blood ketone meter, and a written copy of your pump settings `10.6`

> **Note** `10.note` — Your team’s list comes first. Ask them whether you need ketone strips or glucagon.

### 11 · Who to ask
Group: **Setting up** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

- Your diabetes educator: your plan, your readings and everyday questions. Many are Certified Diabetes Educators (CDE®), licensed health professionals certified in diabetes education `11.1`
- Your doctor: your diagnosis, your prescriptions and your checkups `11.2`
- A pharmacist: what each medicine is for, how to store it, and your sick-day medicine plan `11.3`
- How you’re feeling: your team, or a registered mental health provider from Breakthrough T1D’s Mental Health + Diabetes Directory `11.4`

> **Note** `11.note` — Not sure where to start? Start with your diabetes educator. Some educators in the CDE directory see people without a referral.

*Sources for this card:* Find a CDE® (Canadian Diabetes Educator Certification Board (CDECB)); Stay Safe When You Have Diabetes and Are Sick or at Risk of Dehydration (Diabetes Canada); Getting Started with Insulin (Diabetes Canada); Mental Health Support (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF))

## Referral band

*Sources for the band:* Eye Damage (Diabetic Retinopathy) (Diabetes Canada); Blood Glucose Monitoring in Adults and Children with Diabetes: Update 2021 (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Checking Blood Sugar (Diabetes Canada); Retinopathy (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Chronic Kidney Disease in Diabetes (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Kidney Disease (Diabetes Canada); Foot Care (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Foot care: a step toward good health (08/25) (Diabetes Canada); Find a CDE® (Canadian Diabetes Educator Certification Board (CDECB))

**Your first year** `band.heading`

- **Learning the basics** `band.1` — The first months are for learning, at your own pace. Your diabetes educator can go over your plan, your readings and your questions. With gestational diabetes or prediabetes, your checkups are different, so ask your team which of these apply.
  - **Find a CDE — Canadian Diabetes Educator Certification Board** `band.1.link.1`  
    <https://systems.cdecb.ca/findCDE> · same tab, an English page · shown on /en and /fr  
    *Register:* Find a CDE® (Canadian Diabetes Educator Certification Board (CDECB))
- **About every 3 months: A1C** `band.2` — Diabetes Canada’s guideline suggests an A1C test about every 3 months. For adults whose numbers have been steady at target, your team may space it out. Your usual target is in Your target ranges.
  - *Where card 3's title appears in this body, it links to card 3.*
- **Eyes** `band.3` — Diabetes Canada says to have an eye exam once a year, unless your eye-care professional suggests something different. With type 2, the first one is at diagnosis. With type 1, for people 15 and over, they start 5 years after diagnosis. Children have their own schedule. Your team tells you when yours is due. ✎
- **Kidneys** `band.4` — Diabetes Canada’s guideline says two tests, called ACR and eGFR, check your kidneys at least once a year. With type 2 they start at diagnosis. With type 1 they usually start 5 years after diagnosis. Children have their own schedule, so ask your team.
- **Feet** `band.5` — Diabetes Canada suggests washing, drying and checking your feet every day, with a mirror if you need one. At least once a year, your team checks your bare feet, including feeling and blood flow.

## Questions for the nurse

*Where the Canadian sources disagree, or a line needed a clinical judgement, the copy above uses a default. None of these is settled: each line named under "Where" renders the default today, in both locales. Rule on each one — keep the default, or take the alternative — and the copy is changed to match. Reviewer-only: none of this renders on a page.*

- **N12.** Default used: **Card 2’s doors open the matching Know Your Type cards** (now in use: Ch05 is served, so the `knowYourTypeRoute` hold is lifted, review of 2026-10-05). Type 1 → card 1, type 2 → card 2, prediabetes → card 3, gestational → card 4, less common types → card 6 ("Could my type be different?"), in the page locale.  
  *Where:* `2.fig`  
  *Alternative:* Point the doors at the four existing path pages (`type-1`, `type-2`, `gestational`, `prediabetes`) instead, with the "less common types" door going to Know Your Type card 6.

**Settled by the source check, for the record** — the copy already reflects these; the alternative is still open to the nurse:

- **N3.** Default used: **Settled by the source check.** A1C "about every 3 months", plus "for adults whose numbers have been steady at target, your team may space it out" (Ch9 "at least every 6 months… in adults"). The band does not print the 6-month figure.  
  *Where:* `band.2`  
  *Alternative:* Print "at least every 6 months" as well.
- **N8.** Default used: **Settled by the source check.** Type 1 is now "5 to 10%" (on the DC page), so 5–10% and 90–95% no longer add up to more than 100%.  
  *Where:* `2.1`, `2.2`  
  *Alternative:* "About 10%" (also on the page).
- **N9.** Default used: **Settled by the source check.** The prediabetes definition follows DC’s wording ("higher than normal, but not yet high enough to be… type 2 diabetes").  
  *Where:* `2.4`  
  *Alternative:* Add DC’s "Not everyone with prediabetes will develop type 2 diabetes, but many people will."

**Before publishing — factual checks, not clinical rulings:**

Re-read 2026-10-06 for ruling C17, its section on being ill: check more often, such as every 2–4 hours; about 15 g of carbohydrate from drinks every hour if not eating; under "If you are sick and can’t eat…", call your doctor or go to the emergency room if you vomit or have diarrhea two or more times in 4 hours, and "If you use insulin, keep taking it when you are sick. Re-read 2026-10-06 ("Get coverage for prescription drugs", updated August 18, 2026): "Syringes, lancets, glucometers and other diabetic supplies are not covered by the ODB program"; the ODB program line, "telephone: 416-503-4586 (Toronto area)", "toll-free: 1-888-405-0405" (owner answer B22: the phones on the ODB rows). | `dc-getting-started-with-insulin` | Getting Started with Insulin | Diabetes Canada | Canadian patient education | Paraphrase: rotate sites; insert the pen tip or needle at 90° with a quick smooth motion, and with an 8 or 12 mm needle gently lift the skin or go in at 45° (the page names no 6 mm needle; corrected by the Your Tools source check, 2026-10-05); "Try to use shorter needles with a smaller thickness"; in-use insulin keeps at room temperature up to 30 days; throw out insulin that has been frozen, above 30 °C or expired; storage differs by product, so read the product information; pen tips and lancets go in a sharps container. Ruled 2026-10-06 (C15): the 30 days here is not used, because some labels say 28 (Humalog, Humulin N, Entuzity); the site says most insulins are good for up to 28 days once opened, some for longer, and to follow the leaflet (Diabète Québec). Reviewer evidence on in-use times from the Health Canada monographs (C7): Toujeo 42 days, Humalog 28, Tresiba 56, Awiqli 12 weeks, Entuzity 28. | <https://www.diabetes.ca/living-with-diabetes/blood-sugar-management/getting-started-with-insulin> |

Re-read 2026-10-05 (This Might Be You cards 2 and 3): "we strongly advocate for facilitation of insulin administration in schools and daycares throughout Canada". Re-read 2026-10-06: "Pregnancy is excluded from this guideline as recommendations are being updated separately" (why This Might Be You card 1’s note dates the pregnancy chapter, ruling C23); it "updates the glycemic management portions" of chapter 34 only (C37). Ruled 2026-10-06: C1 3.9 site-wide, 4.0 only for driving; C13 the site uses Ch14 Table 4’s 150 mL (⅔ cup), not this sheet’s ½ cup (125 mL); C29 this sheet’s 4 Life Savers differs from the 6 in Ch14, Drive Safe and Diabète Québec, and the brand is left out; C18 honey is hidden for children, and the babies-under-1 note is sourced to Health Canada (hc-infant-botulism). | <https://www.diabetes.ca/getContentAsset/7f36723d-3507-4657-a579-78b1fd0437e6/0f6cf596-933c-4f74-b36a-77091c512445/hypoglycemia-low-blood-sugar-in-adults.pdf?language=en> |

It also recommends counselling on hypoglycemia for people on insulin who drink (Every Day Living 4.items.3). | `dc-technology-and-devices` | Technology & Devices | Diabetes Canada | Canadian patient education | Paraphrase: intermittently scanned vs real-time CGM; a sensor is slower than blood by up to 15 minutes, so keep a meter as a backup; pumps and hybrid closed loop; pump users keep backup rapid-acting insulin pens or syringes and ketone strips. Re-read word for word by the Your Tools source check (2026-10-05), which confirmed the backup line ("Rapid-acting insulin pens or syringes, Long-acting insulin (if needed), Extra pump supplies (infusion sets, reservoirs), Ketone testing strips… or a ketone blood monitor"; make "a pump backup plan before one is needed") and found: even if offered a CGM, keep a meter and strips for double-checking CGM readings and as a backup; a sensor sits on the skin "like a small, lightweight, waterproof patch… held in place by sticky material", with a small flexible filament; intermittently scanned CGM reads "only when the sensor is scanned", real-time CGM has alarms for low and high sugar levels; some CGMs connect to an insulin pump (a hybrid closed loop system); "Tech isn't for everyone"; readings can be shared from a smartphone with the diabetes team; the difference from a finger check is "more likely to be larger when you're eating or exercising", and a finger check gives the most accurate result; pens are preloaded, with a tip added for each injection and one pen per type of insulin; today's syringes are smaller, use thinner needles and cost less than pens and pumps; a pump gives insulin 24 hours a day through a small tube; the team decides whether a pump will work for you and your pump settings. | <https://www.diabetes.ca/living-with-diabetes/blood-sugar-management/technology-and-devices> |
